### E578 — R1 landed: the plan requests, the caller grants, admission binds (2026-11-20)

**S1+S2+S3 of E577.** The plan can no longer own its own waiver, and the caller can now issue one. Landed as one
step because S1 alone would have made the parser refuse documents the tool could not yet produce.

| Layer | Change | Rule that fires |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Grammar (`plan_v2.py`) | `DISPOSITION-OWNER` / `DISPOSITION-EVIDENCE` in plan text are refused **before** the reason vocabulary is consulted, so the document is told the real defect. `_admit_evidence` now accepts a request (`reason` present) as structurally sufficient; whether it was *granted* is admission's question | `disposition-not-caller-authority` |
| Grant (`plan_admission.py`) | `EvidenceRef` + `DispositionDeclaration` + `parse_dispositions` (shape, closed vocabulary, typed evidence, ISO date, ≤16, one grant per reason) and `bind_dispositions` (undeclared, stale, future, then copies owner + canonical reference onto the invariant) | `disposition-invalid`, `-reason-unratified`, `-owner-invalid`, `-evidence-invalid`, `-reviewed-at-invalid`, `-too-many`, `-duplicate-reason`, `-undeclared`, `-review-stale` |
| Tool (`workflow_tool.py`) | New closed `dispositions` parameter (4 fields, `additionalProperties: false`); refused outside `CREATE_NEW` before shape is judged; parsed with the same function admission uses | `dispositions_require_create`, `invalid_dispositions` |
| Controller | `AcquisitionSubstrateRequest`/`AcquisitionSubstrate`/`WorkflowContext` carry the grant; `_install_bootstrap_project_with_detail` binds **before** `prepare_bundle`, so an unauthorised body never becomes a project. The precise rule goes to the log; the record keeps the existing `bootstrap/invalid-body` code | `bootstrap-invalid-body` |

Notes that matter later:

* **`maxItems` is not provider-portable** (`registry._PORTABLE_SCHEMA_KEYS`), so the 16-grant cap is published as
  prose in the schema and enforced in `parse_dispositions`. A schema that cannot say the limit must not imply
  there is none — the validator is the gate, the same split the slug already uses.
* **Staleness is checked on every grant, not on every used grant**: a 31-day-old grant is refused even if the plan
  does not reference it, because the thing that expired is the review.
* **Authorisation happens once, at install.** Later runs re-parse the installed bytes without declarations and
  never rebind: the plan was authorised by the run that installed it, and a re-admission that could re-grant would
  be a second authorisation.

**Not yet landed — stated so it is not overclaimed.** The reference is *typed and parsed*, but **no byte is read**:
`doc:<path>@sha256:<hex>` is not yet checked for existence or digest match, so today a grant can name a file that
does not exist and still bind. That is S4 (next), and until it lands the honest description of the system is
"evidence is typed, not verified". `issue:` and `review:` stay attested-with-reference by design (no egress).

**S5 is folded into D-V2-7.** No prompt needs editing yet: `ACQUISITION_SYSTEM_PROMPT` mentions no disposition at
all, and the model's *semantics* schema is what will carry the request once the renderer exists.

### E579 — R6 closed: a `doc:` grant is verified against the pinned bytes (2026-11-20)

**S4 of E577, and the correction E578 promised.** E578 shipped the reference *typed but unread*: a grant could name
a file that did not exist and still bind. That gap is closed here.

| Fact | Rule | Where |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| The pinned view does not hold the path | `disposition-evidence-missing` | `_resolve_granted_evidence`, before `bind_dispositions` |
| The path is one the substrate refuses to name (absolute, `..`, empty segment, NUL, backslash) | `disposition-evidence-invalid` | same, via `port_relative` → `WorkspacePortError("invalid_request")` |
| The file needs more than one bounded port read | `disposition-evidence-invalid` | `PortRead.eof` is `False` — a digest over a prefix is not a digest over the file |
| The bytes are not the bytes that were reviewed | `disposition-evidence-mismatch` | `PortRead.sha256` vs the declared digest |
| There is no pinned view at all | `disposition-evidence-unresolvable` | a doc grant is refused rather than trusted |
| `issue:` / `review:` | — | no read, no resolution, no claim: typed reference, reported as attested |

Order matters and is deliberate: **resolve, then bind, then install.** A grant whose bytes cannot be checked never
reaches `bind_dispositions`, so no invariant can carry an owner granted by an unverified reference. The read is the
substrate's own bounded read (`PORT_READ_MAX_BYTES`), not a new file-reading path in the controller — the same view
the run uses for everything else, so "verified against the revision this run sees" is true by construction.

**Why `issue:`/`review:` still authorise.** This system has no egress; a real check is impossible. The honest choice
is either to refuse them (which would make the ratified reason set unusable for `OWNER_APPROVAL`, the one reason
whose evidence is a conversation) or to accept them as *typed references* and never report them as verified. The
second is what R2's `ATTESTED` exists for: `attested` names the contract, and the record's `evidence` names what
backed it — the reader sees `issue:FIRST-42`, not a green tick.

**Verification.** `tests/test_ai_native_dispositions.py` 47 (+8 resolver oracles), `test_ai_native_bootstrap.py` 37
(+6 end-to-end at the pre-install gate). **Mutants 6/6 killed** (`/tmp/mut_step5.py`), including one that never
compares the digest and one that never reads at all. Full suite `8205 passed, 18 skipped, 3 xfailed` with the three
baseline-red tests deselected; `ruff` clean over 653 files, `mypy` clean over 222 sources.

### E580 — R3 landed: the policy matrix, and one waiver frees one claim (2026-11-20)

**Operator approved the matrix as proposed.** Enforced in `plan_v2._admit_evidence`, because both facts are properties
of the graph: no caller input is needed to know that a preservation claim has no test, or that one granted invariant
backs several contracts.

| `class` × `kind` | Before | Now |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| any class, covered by a selector | executable | executable (unchanged) |
| `PRESERVATION`, uncovered — **any** kind, **any** evidence mode | a `HARD` one was refused only as a generic `hard-contract-without-executable-evidence`; a `SOFT` one was silently admissible; a disposition could carry it | `preservation-without-executable-evidence` |
| `FUNCTIONAL` / `CONSTRAINT`, `HARD`, uncovered | needs a disposition | unchanged |
| `FUNCTIONAL` / `CONSTRAINT`, `SOFT`, uncovered | allowed | allowed (unchanged) — the matrix tightens preservation and clusters, it does not make `SOFT` executable |
| two or more uncovered contracts leaning on one granted invariant | one decision attested the whole cluster | `disposition-covers-several-contracts` |

**Why `PRESERVATION` is the strict cell.** It is the claim "what worked still works", and it is the only claim a test
can *always* express — a regression test for existing behaviour needs no host, no deployment identity, no operator
approval. The whole ratified reason set (`HOST_READINESS`, `DEPLOYMENT_IDENTITY`, `OWNER_APPROVAL`,
`DURABILITY_POWER_LOSS`) is about things outside the sandbox; none of them is an excuse for not testing that something
still works. Attesting preservation away is exactly how a regression ships green. This also agrees with the existing
CT54 exemption in `slice_verification` (a preservation contract is exempt from *kill directives* because "their proof
is an existing test or an absence") — that exemption assumed a test exists; now the grammar says so.

**Why the cluster bound.** G4's second half: a single grant on one invariant could free every contract hanging off it,
so the decision the caller made once ("host readiness is out of scope for a test") silently became a decision about
claims it never named. The bound counts claims *leaning* on the grant, not everything it mentions, so a tested
contract on a granted invariant stays executable and does not consume the waiver.

**Consequence worth recording.** Two R2 test fixtures had to change: they put two contracts on one disposed invariant,
which is now refused. That is the rule working, not a test being bent — `attested_contracts` still reports every
contract, and the seal still names them; what changed is that a plan can no longer *manufacture* such a cluster.

### E581 — Plan corrections from the source audit: P0-1…P3-4, and the renderer's contract (2026-11-20)

The operator asked for the found defects to be written into the plan before implementation. Every row in §12 of
`notes/i03-ai-native-workflow-refactor-plan-v2.md` was reproduced by running production code; none is inferred from a
document. The register is now the plan's, so a later entry closes a row rather than re-describing it.

**What changed in the plan.**

| Section | Change |
|---|---|
| §2 grammar block | Two positional facts recorded, both previously got wrong: `STEPS: <mode>` is the single mode line (a second, empty `STEPS:` header is `slice-<n>-steps-mode`), and a step line is a slice-level list item that must not sit inside `STEP-EXIT-CHECKS:`. Plus the **D-V2-7 structure**: planner returns typed semantics, controller renders every byte, selectors are carried *project-relative* and expanded only at render, and the renderer refuses to emit a pair that would not parse. |
| §2 SLICE2 open items | The CT-2.1 remainder now names **both** planner-carried slugs (`project_slug` *and* `increment_slug`), and records the D-V2-7 order: renderer → prompt → payload wiring, with P0-2/P2-2 fixed in the third step because they are the same route decision. |
| CT table | CT-2.3 gained the renderer law; **CT-2.6** added — the prompt must be written in the payload's vocabulary and carry one example payload the real chain accepts. |
| §12 (new) | The defect register, with stable ids and measured evidence. |

**The two defects that matter.** P0-1: a body written exactly as `ACQUISITION_SYSTEM_PROMPT` instructs is refused by
`parse_plan` — the prompt teaches V1 `Schema-4` Markdown that the PLAN-V2 route no longer admits, so the first real
create-new cannot produce an admissible plan. P0-2: a V2 project cannot be resumed, because `resolve_existing_choice`
snapshots with the default `PLAN-V1` while only the bootstrap branch sets `PLAN_V2`; the route is one-way and D-V2-2's
"no V1 fallback" is true only in the direction that has been built.

**P1-1/P1-2 are policy, not typos, and are deliberately not folded into the renderer.** After R1 a reason is a
*request*; `contract_evidence` still grades `ATTESTED` from the reason alone, so an ungranted graph can name contracts
attested, and `bind_dispositions`' returned graph is discarded. The cluster bound is likewise per invariant, so one
grant can authorise two invariants that share a reason. Both are recorded with the reproduced evidence and a preferred
fix (grade on the bound grant; refuse a repeated reason), to be ratified as one decision rather than slipped in
underneath a refactor.

### E582 — P0-1 closed: the planner authors semantics and one renderer owns every byte (2026-11-20)

**The defect.** `ACQUISITION_SYSTEM_PROMPT` taught the retired V1 `Schema-4` Markdown while the
new-project route admits only `PLAN-V2`. A body written exactly as instructed was refused
(`plan-format-marker-roadmap`; with the marker `slice-1-unknown-field`), so the first real
create-new could not produce an admissible plan. The prompt and the parser were two descriptions
of one grammar, and only one of them was true.

**Landed — D-V2-7 step 1, and the prompt of step 2.**

| Layer | Change | Proof |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `plan_semantics.py` (new) | Typed payload (`PlanSemantics`, `Question`, `SemanticsSlice`, `SemanticsContract`, `SemanticsStep`), `parse_semantics`, `render_roadmap`/`render_increment`/`render_open_questions`/`render_project`, `from_graph`. Selectors travel **project-relative** and are expanded only at render, because the slug is caller authority and can still be substituted. | 26 tests, laws + refusals |
| Self-check | `parse_semantics` renders through a **probe slug** and `render_project` re-parses with the real one, so the renderer cannot emit bytes admission rejects and the payload is judged by the grammar's own vocabulary — no second copy of the rules. | mutants M2, M6 |
| Wire (`managed_acquisition.py`) | `BOOTSTRAP_NEW_PROJECT` carries `semantics` and nothing else; the retired `roadmap_body`/`increment_body` are a closed-key refusal. `BootstrapNewProjectChoice.semantics` holds the payload; the prose fields remain for the V1 route only. | M10, M11 |
| Controller | `_bootstrap_bodies` is the one place the renderer is consulted, and it is called **before** the route gate so the bytes admission judges and the bytes installed are the same object. `_rendered_increment_sha256` takes the same path, so a refusal record cannot name a document the install never wrote. | M8, M9 |
| Prompt | Rewritten in the payload's terms: imperative rules, closed vocabularies, both refusal codes named, one worked payload. The retired shapes are gone, not left beside the new one. | CT-2.6 test walks the prompt's own example through parse → render → parse |

**Two defects found while building it, both real and both now closed.**

1. **Selector traversal was admitted.** `_SELECTOR_RE`'s character class includes `.` and `/`, so
   `worklogs/w/acceptance/tests/../../../etc/x.py::test_a` parsed cleanly — while the plan requires
   `..` and symlink escape to be rejected. `_FORBIDDEN_SEGMENTS` now refuses empty/`.`/`..` segments;
   the test drives the payload path and the raw grammar.
2. **The round-trip law caught my own fixture.** The first seeded corpus left contracts uncovered,
   which is a legitimate `hard-contract-without-executable-evidence` refusal — the corpus was wrong,
   not the renderer. The law is what surfaced it; a spot check on one example would not have.

**Honest limits, stated so they are not overclaimed.**

* The roadmap has no byte-idempotence law: it carries two prose sections the graph does not model.
  Only the increment is byte-idempotent, which is the half a seal digest covers.
* `render_project` returns three documents; `ledger.md` stays with the authority (it is a fixed
  harness body, not semantics), and `acceptance/` materialization is SLICE3 (P2-1).
* The payload is validated but **nothing is installed from it yet end-to-end on a live host** —
  that is SLICE2's managed-run DoD, not this step.
* `from_graph` normalises step marks to `[ ]`; ticks never enter sealed bytes (Q-V2-STATUS-1).

invoke/managed-acquisition/prompt coherence). **Mutants 11/11 killed** (`tests/mutation/mut_step7.py`)

### E583 — P0-2 blocked on Q-V2-RESUME-1: how does a *resuming* run learn the grammar? (2026-11-20)

P0-1 is closed (E582). Before touching `resolve_existing_choice` I re-measured the defect from the
CT-2.6 prompt payload rather than from the register text, because the register's evidence line was
written by the audit, not by me. Three measurements changed the shape of the fix:

1. **The failure is silent admission, not a diagnostic.** `render_bundle` + `resolve_existing_choice`
   on a valid V2 pair returns `ResolvedExistingIncrement` with `format=PLAN-V1`, `format_error=None`
   and `graph is None`. The register predicted outcome `DIAGNOSTICS`; what actually happens is that a
   V2 increment is reported as a *well-formed V1 plan*. A caller cannot distinguish this from a real
   V1 project by any field it receives.
2. **Identity metadata is grammar-neutral.** Both installed documents carry V1-shaped front matter
   (`Roadmap-ID`, `Increment-ID`, `status`, `slices`, `shipped`) and `parse_artifact_metadata` accepts
   them unchanged. So the format question is *not* an artifact-metadata question, and a resolver fix
   cannot be smuggled in as "the parser understood it".
3. **The marker is already in the bytes and the parser already requires it.** `plan_v2.parse_plan`
   raises `plan-format-marker-roadmap` when it is absent; `plan_semantics._MARKER` writes it. So a
   V2 document is self-identifying *to the V2 parser*, which is exactly why reading it feels natural
   and exactly why it collides with the ratified text.

That collision is the blocker, and it is not mine to resolve:

* §2 and CT-1.1: "The format is chosen by the **route**, never by sniffing the document."
* D-V2-2: "No V1 fallback, **no marker dispatch**, no parallel code path."
* `PlanSnapshot` docstring: "``format`` comes from the caller's route, and only the caller's route."
* But a resuming route observes an *installed* document it did not render. There is no route-local
  fact that distinguishes a V2 project from a V1 one, because §12 SLICE1 deliberately made the
  bootstrap route one-way.

So P0-2 is not a one-line parameter. It is **Q-V2-RESUME-1**, filed in the plan's decision table with
three bounded options:

* **A — refuse.** `AUTO_SELECT_EXISTING` never admits V2; a V2 install is terminal until SLICE5
  retires the legacy route. Smallest code, but it closes P0-2 as *refused*, and it would make the
  first create-new project unresumable on a live host.
* **B — runtime pin + whole-document marker validation.** The resolver reads `Plan-Format:`; the
  pinned runtime owns the vocabulary; missing/duplicate/mismatched/V1 are refused, never dispatched.
  It is reading a *declared version field*, which is a genuinely different act from content sniffing,
  but the difference has to be written into the ratified text, not assumed by the implementer.
* **C — authority-recorded format at install.** Cleanest, and it makes the answer structural rather
  than textual. It is not available today: `acceptance_bundle.py` has no production caller (only
  `kill_attribution`, `acceptance_defect`, `acceptance_collection` and tests import it), so the seal
  anchor Q-V2-BOOT-1/D-V2-5 describes does not yet exist to read. C would push P0-2 behind SLICE2/3.

**Also noted while grounding (not fixed, not in scope):** `resolve_existing_choice` demands
`format` never be inferred, yet it also returns a V1 snapshot for a document it cannot have decided
about — so the sibling weaker case already exists for V1. Whatever is ratified should state the rule
once for both grammars rather than patch only the V2 branch.

**Decision:** stop, do not guess. Q-V2-RESUME-1 is a new policy decision touching two ratified
constraints; per the stop/escalate rule it is escalated with context, impact and options rather than
implemented under an assumed reading. No `src/` change in this step; the only edits are the plan's
decision table and this register row. P1-1/P1-2 remain ready to start and are **not** blocked by this
question — they need no revisit of what "format" means.

### E584 — correction: P0-2 was mis-framed; the V2 route already behaves correctly (2026-11-20)

E583 escalated P0-2 as a policy question about *where a resuming run learns the grammar*. That was the
wrong question, and the operator's challenge — "distinguish a defect from correct behaviour; there is
one V1 plan that is becoming legacy, every new project will be V2; what matters is that a new plan
validates correctly and malformed input errors" — is the right test. Run against the production code:

| On the route that declares V2 | Result |
|---|---|
| valid V2 pair | `format=PLAN-V2`, `format_error=None`, `graph` present |
| V1 document on the V2 route | refused: `plan-format-marker-roadmap` |
| malformed V2 | refused: `unknown-top-level-section` |

That is the requirement, and it holds. `tests/test_ai_native_plan_v2.py::test_v2_document_is_never_judged_by_v1_validators`
(CT-1.3) is the standing executable proof.

**Three errors of mine, named:**

1. **I promoted a register row to a requirement.** "A `PLAN-V2` project cannot be resumed" is an audit
   observation about a route, not a product requirement. I asked how to satisfy it instead of whether
   the scenario exists.
2. **I invented a decision that was already ratified.** §2/§40 already says the trusted runtime pins the
   supported V2 grammar and rejects unsupported/missing/mixed/V1 *before coder*. Rejection is not marker
   dispatch, so no new policy was needed. Filing it as a new question implied the plan was silent.
3. **I treated a correct legacy behaviour as a bug.** `resolve_existing_choice` returning `PLAN-V1` for a
   V1 project is correct today, because the legacy grammar is legal until D-V2-2 retires the route. My
   "silent admission" finding is real *behaviour* but not a *defect* on any supported route.

**Why the marker concern was misplaced anyway.** `plan_semantics._MARKER` is a renderer constant, and
`publication._METADATA_LINE` refuses a planner-supplied `Plan-Format:` line, so the marker can never be
model-authored. A rule that reads it is therefore not trusting the document's content — the exact thing
INV-01 forbids — it is reading a field only the harness can write.

**Disposition.** Q-V2-RESUME-1 withdrawn (kept as a visible withdrawn row). P0-2 re-scoped to SLICE5
legacy-route retirement: when the existing-project route stops being fed by legacy projects, it must
either honour the runtime-pinned marker or refuse, and that rides the retirement's own negative control.
No code change now. P1-1/P1-2 are next.

**Re-verification the operator asked for ("проверь все еще раз"), on a rebuilt environment** (the
sandbox had lost `.venv` and the branch pointer; worktree bytes were proven identical to
`origin/arena/51e929de-first-agent-dev` before resetting to it):

* Full suite: **8246 passed, 18 skipped, 3 xfailed, 9 deselected** in 637.77s (0:10:37). The collection
  size is unchanged from E582: `8244+18+3+11 = 8246+18+3+9 = 8276`. The passed/deselected split moved by
  two only because of which `--deselect` nodeids this run passed on the command line, **not** because any
  test was added or removed — an earlier draft of this entry claimed "two tests added while grounding
  P0-2", and that claim was wrong; it is corrected here before anyone relies on it.
* P0-1 mutants re-run from scratch: **11/11 killed** (`tests/mutation/mut_step7.py`), same kill list.
* Environment rebuilt by `scripts/arena-env-build.sh`; `ENVIRONMENT_CHECK_OK` (CPython 3.13.16).

**My error, and the cost.** E583 cost one commit and one escalation cycle. The mitigation that would
have caught it: before filing a Q, ask "which *route* would exercise this, and is it a supported route
today?" A defect that needs an unsupported route to manifest is a sequencing item, not a blocker.

### E585 — P1-1 and P1-2 closed: a verdict may never be stronger than its evidence (2026-11-20)

One root cause, two symptoms, both reproduced on production code before any edit:

| | Reproduced as | Cause |
|---|---|---|
| **P1-1** | `parse_plan` alone reports `attested_contracts == ('CT-1.1',)` for a graph nobody granted | `contract_evidence` graded `ATTESTED` from `evidence == NON_EXECUTABLE`, which after R1 is only the plan's **request** |
| **P1-2** | two invariants naming `HOST_READINESS` + **one** caller declaration → `('CT-1.1', 'CT-1.2')` | the grant is keyed by *reason*, so one decision authorised two claims |

**P1-2 was mis-diagnosed in the register, and the correction matters.** §12 said "the
cluster bound is per invariant, not per grant" — but R3/E580 had already fixed exactly
that (`disposition-covers-several-contracts`). The real hole is one level down: R3 bounds
*contracts per invariant*, while the authorisation travels by *reason*, which the plan may
reuse freely. So a plan could reach R3's bound and still spend one decision on two
different invariants. The fix is a one-shot reason at the point where the request is
parsed (`_parse_invariants` → `disposition-reason-reused`), deliberately placed on the
*invariant* so it stays orthogonal to the cluster rule: a first attempt put it on the
contract loop and turned the cluster refusal into the wrong diagnosis, which a surviving
mutant caught (M4 in `tests/mutation/mut_step8.py`).

**P1-1 had a second half the register did not name.** Fixing the grading alone would have
been cosmetic: the controller *did* bind the dispositions before the install, then
**discarded the result** (`bind_dispositions(...)` with no assignment), and
`_admit_installed_plan` re-parsed the installed bytes with no declarations. So even a
legitimately granted contract reached the seal as merely uncovered. Two changes:

* `contract_evidence` grades `ATTESTED` only when the invariant carries the grant
  (`owner is not None`) — the observable trace `bind_dispositions` leaves.
* the granted graph is carried across the install as `authorised` and reconciled by
  `_authorised_graph`, which requires the installed plan to equal the authorised plan
  **minus its grant fields**. Comparison is by graph, not by byte digest, because the
  authority wraps the same prose in its own front matter, so the digest differs by
  design; anything else returns `None` and the snapshot keeps its request-only graph.
  E577's "authorised once, at install, never rebound" is unchanged: this carries the
  *existing* grant forward, it never mints a new one.

**Prompt.** `ACQUISITION_SYSTEM_PROMPT` already said "one grant backs one claim" for the
cluster rule; it now names both directions and both rule codes, and the coherence bank
pins that it does. A rule the model is never told is a rule it learns by being refused.

**Verification.** `tests/test_ai_native_plan_v2.py` 92 (+8), `test_s5p1_acquisition_substrate.py`
12 (+2, the real seam: a pinned view over the installed tree, asserting the grant reaches
`admission.snapshot.graph`), `test_ai_native_acceptance_bundle.py` 95, coherence 27.
**Mutants 8/8 killed** (`tests/mutation/mut_step8.py`) — plus one mutant recorded as
*equivalent* rather than counted: the `graph is None` guard in `_authorised_graph` is
redundant with the comparison that follows (`None != PlanGraph`), and exists for type
narrowing, so no test could kill it without observing something the code does not do.
Two fixture sets were rebased rather than bent: the grading tests now use a `granted_graph`
helper, because the seal grades *granted* evidence and the old fixtures graded requests.
Full suite **8256 passed, 18 skipped, 3 xfailed, 9 deselected**; `ruff` clean; `mypy src`
clean over 223 sources.

### E586 — P2-2 closed: the planner authors content, never identity (2026-11-20)

The register said "`initial-plan` is not fixed… `choice.increment_slug` still comes from the
planner's JSON". Grounding found the premise was right but the mechanism was worse than
described, and one part of the register's story was already dead code.

**What was actually true.** Both installed documents keep V1-shaped front matter, so:

* `_bootstrap_bodies` on the V2 route returns `render_project`'s hard-coded key
  `increments/increment-01-initial-plan.md` — the planner's `increment_slug` never reached
  the rendered *body*.
* but `render_bundle` was called with `choice.increment_slug` from the planner, so the file
  *path* was model-chosen. Measured: `increment_slug="my-own-name"` produced
  `worklogs/demo-project/increments/increment-01-my-own-name.md`. The plan says three times
  that the slug is harness-fixed, and admission reads that path.
* `_with_project_hint` overwrote a planner-written `project_slug` and logged a warning — a
  substitution the model never saw and the operator could not audit.

**Also dead, and now documented as such.** `roadmap_body`/`increment_body` are populated
nowhere in `src/`: the wire parser only ever built `semantics`, and the controller flips
`plan_format = PLAN_V2` on every bootstrap branch before any bytes exist. So a V1 bootstrap
through the wire already refused with `payload-missing`; the V1 prose path survives only in
`tests/test_s5p1_bootstrap.py`, which drives the controller directly with `plan_format`
left at its default — a state no production route can reach.

**The change (as ratified in §12/CT-2.1, "the proposal/resolved split").**

| | Before | Now |
|---|---|---|
| wire | `{kind, project_slug, increment_slug, semantics}` | `{kind, semantics}` |
| parser returns | `BootstrapNewProjectChoice` | `BootstrapProposal` (no name fields) |
| planner names a slug | silently overridden | `selection/choice-malformed` |
| increment | planner's string → bundle path | `INITIAL_INCREMENT_SLUG = "initial-plan"` |
| controller | `_with_project_hint` | `_resolve_bootstrap_identity`, `None` when the caller named nothing |

**One mistake caught by the suite, worth recording.** My first version of the
"no caller slug" refusal returned `project-route-mismatch` unconditionally and broke two
lifecycle tests that expected `bootstrap-unavailable`. The tests were right and I was
wrong: `_install_bootstrap_project_with_detail` checks *authority* before *route*, because
"fix the body" (or "name the project") sends an operator one step in the wrong direction
when the run has no managed execution at all. The early guard now mirrors the installer's
order, so the same fact gets the same rule whichever checkpoint sees it first.

**Verification.** `tests/test_managed_acquisition.py` 98 (+3: both identity fields, and
both together), `test_ai_native_bootstrap.py` 37 (the real managed run now installs
`increment-01-initial-plan.md` and proves the planner's name never lands),
`test_admission_v2_provenance.py` 29, lifecycle 24, coherence 27.
**Mutants 6/6 killed** (`tests/mutation/mut_step9.py`) after one survivor: M6 showed the
coherence bank did not pin the prompt's *prohibition*, only its omission — a model not told
otherwise will helpfully supply a slug, so the negative sentence is now asserted.
Full suite **8259 passed, 18 skipped, 3 xfailed, 9 deselected**; `ruff` clean; `mypy src`
clean over 223 sources. Two banks were rebased rather than bent: every bootstrap payload in
`test_admission_v2_provenance.py` (5) and the lifecycle `BOOTSTRAP` fixture lost their
identity keys, because a payload carrying them is now malformed *before* the route refusal
those tests exist to prove.

### E587 — P2-3 closed: the create route authors, it does not choose (D-V2-9 steps 2–5)

**What landed.** `PlannerDispatchKind.CREATE_NEW_PROJECT` — a third writing kind that carries
exactly one directory (`authoring_root = worklogs/<slug>`), built by the controller from the
caller's slug and validated in `__post_init__` (two components, `worklogs` first, no
`active_plan`). `_stage_planner_dispatch` chooses it from the *route*, so a create-authorized
run stops being an acquisition stage at all: `ACQUISITION` pins a reader and offers no writer,
which is precisely what a planner that must author documents cannot use.

**The scaffold is harness bytes and nothing else.** `project_scaffold.py` returns the seven
files of D-V2-9.7, written by the stage through its own port before the first tool call, with
`roadmap.md` first because its create-only write is the collision check. Two constraints that
look stylistic are forced: `.gitkeep` is impossible (`_parts` rejects `""`/`.`/`..` and the
writer has no mkdir), so `notes/` and `reviews/` are carried by `README.md`; and the
placeholder test module defines no test function, because a placeholder *test* is a fake
green. The unfilled pair is refused by `parse_plan` (`missing-slice`) — verified directly
rather than assumed, since a scaffold that parsed would be a plan nobody wrote.

**The metadata table (D-V2-9.3) is deliberately small.** `project_metadata.check_project_metadata`
walks fields that must *agree with something else*: `Roadmap-ID` vs the path slug, the
increment id vs `active-increment`, one `created` across the project, `status` membership
only. A legal `status` is the planner's choice and every value in the vocabulary passes —
that is what "as flexible as it can be while still being a check" (Q#10) means in code.
Refusals map to the existing recorded rule `bootstrap/invalid-metadata`; the specific
mismatch goes to the log, because the admission vocabulary is closed and already names the
event.

**Collision is `bootstrap/collision`, not `stale`.** The authority would refuse the
scaffold's first write with `STALE_REVISION` — correct mechanism, useless message: an agent
reads "stale" as its own lost race. The check therefore runs before any view opens, from the
pinned inventory that already drove the route (complete *and* incomplete directories both
collide).

**P2-3 is closed by deletion, not by a patch.** The old task text told the model "return
`BOOTSTRAP_NEW_PROJECT` with exactly that `project_slug`" while `_parse_bootstrap_choice`
demanded `{"kind","semantics"}` — a model following the instruction was guaranteed
`choice-malformed`. Both halves are gone with the payload route from this stage's task. The
test that missed it asserted the phrase `caller: <slug>`; it is rewritten to assert the
*absence* of the payload instruction, which is the property that would have caught the drift.

**Verification.** 503 tests across the touched banks (`test_ai_native_project_scaffold.py`
18 new, `test_s5p1_acquisition_lifecycle.py` +5, `test_ai_native_bootstrap.py` rewritten
route-text oracles); `ruff` clean; `mypy src` clean over 225 sources. **Mutants 3/3 killed:**
dropping the `active-increment` cross-check, reordering the scaffold so `roadmap.md` is not
first, and disabling the collision check. The third survived the first version of its test,
which only observed "something refused" — it now asserts no stage was dispatched at all,
which is the property that separates *refused* from *ran and lost the work*.

**Not done here, deliberately.** D-V2-9.8 (repair as a second authoring stage) stays its own
CT/slice per the operator. Steps 1 (payload deletion) and 6 (prompt rewrite) remain: step 1
is a pure deletion once step 6 can be written truthfully, and the operator's ordering put
P2-4 last.

### E588 — P2-4 closed: the payload layer is gone, and the create route is one publication (2026-11-21)

**What was deleted, and why it could be deleted rather than kept.** P2-4's deletion list was
~3 600 lines across six files. The safe version of that work is not "remove the code" but
"prove the code is unreachable first", so that is what this entry is about. The create route
now dispatches `CREATE_NEW_PROJECT`, and `_authored_stage_result` returns before
`_stage_acquisition_choice` ever runs; `_resolve_bootstrap_identity` could therefore only be
reached with `hint is None` (where it returns `None`) or with a slug (where the route had
already taken the authoring path). The whole install chain — `_bootstrap_bodies`,
`_rendered_increment_sha256`, `_install_bootstrap_project_with_detail`,
`_install_bootstrap_project`, `_admit_installed_plan`, `_authorised_graph`,
`_resolve_bootstrap_identity` — was dead before it was deleted. `plan_semantics.py` (573
lines) went with it: its only live importer was the payload half of
`managed_acquisition.py`, which is also gone (`BootstrapProposal`, `_parse_bootstrap_choice`,
`BootstrapNewProjectChoice`, `AcquisitionOutcome.bootstrap`).

**Two properties nearly died with the deletions, and that is the real finding.** Deleting the
installer silently took `_resolve_granted_evidence` (R6: a `doc:` grant must match the pinned
bytes) and `bind_dispositions` (R1: an unbound `NON_EXECUTABLE` invariant is a *request*, not
an attestation) out of every live path. Both were only ever called from inside
`_install_bootstrap_project_with_detail`. Nothing failed: `bind_dispositions` has no caller
nowhere, and `contract_evidence` grades an owner-less invariant as `UNCOVERED`, so the
regression would have been a plan that reached the coder with its dispositions silently
unbound. They are restored in `_admit_published_project` — `_granted_dispositions` verifies
the digests through the same pinned view, and the granted graph is bound to the snapshot the
route actually admits. The authoring route is in fact *stronger* than the install path was:
there is one parse, so a grant cannot be re-pointed at a different read-back.

**A dead arm and a lie in a comment.** Removing the installer also removed the only thing that
refused `BOOTSTRAP_NEW_PROJECT` on a select-only route. The first fix was an arm in
`_bind_acquisition_admission`; it worked, but it was reached only if `parse_acquisition_choice`
still produced that kind, and `AcquisitionOutcome.bootstrap` had just been deleted — the arm
was unreachable. The refusal now lives where the shape is read:
`parse_acquisition_choice` raises `AcquisitionChoiceError("bootstrap", "retired-choice")`, a
new closed rule in the `bootstrap` validator. That is earlier, more accurate, and it keeps the
route contradiction a *pre-coder* fact instead of a route surprise.

**Prompt rewrite (step 6), and the P0-1 shape of it.** `ACQUISITION_SYSTEM_PROMPT` was 7 168
characters whose spine was "emit one raw JSON object" with a worked `BOOTSTRAP_NEW_PROJECT`
payload. Every word of that is now wrong for the create route, and the route had no prompt of
its own — it was handed a read-only selector's instructions while holding a write view. The
create route gets `AUTHORING_SYSTEM_PROMPT` (Markdown documents, the closed metadata rules,
"do not emit a JSON choice"); the acquisition prompt drops to 2 379 characters and two shapes.
One test asserts the two texts name the same files, because P0-1 was exactly a disagreement
between the task block and the parser.

**Verification.** 398 tests across the touched banks; full suite run with the two environment
gates excluded (86 environment failures on this sandbox, unchanged from the base commit —
`uv`, `semgrep` and `pyrefly` are absent). `ruff` clean; `mypy src` clean over **224** sources
(one fewer: `plan_semantics.py` is gone); doc-links 369 OK. **Mutants 4/4 killed** on the new
rules (the retired shape parsing again; the metadata check deleted from admission; a missing
authored pair reported as "unreadable"; the authoring refusal carrying no durable diagnostic),
plus the surviving step-8 set **4/4** after its four install-path mutants were retired with
the code they mutated.

**The mutant that mattered.** M2 — "admission trusts the published bytes without the metadata
check" — survived the first version of its test, and survived again after a test was added
that called `check_project_metadata` directly. Both tests were proving the *table*, not its
*use*: the scaffold's own front matter is valid, so the happy path cannot tell "checked" from
"not checked", and the direct test never entered admission. The killing test drives
`_admit_published_project` through a pinned view holding a pair that **parses** and is
**still refused** — the increment names a roadmap other than the one in its own directory,
which is a fact the grammar cannot see. That is the difference between testing a rule and
testing that the run consults it.

**Not done here, deliberately.** D-V2-9.8 (repair as a second authoring stage) stays its own
CT/slice per the operator. `prepare_bundle`/`install_project` remain in the authority for
their other callers, as the plan directs; the create route simply stops calling them.

### E592 — repair is a second authoring stage, not the candidate buffer (D-V2-9.8)

The source said this before I wrote it: `seed_plan_candidate` refuses any kind but
`ADMISSION_REPAIR`/`EVAL_REPLAN`, writes **one** draft under `.fa/admission/<run>/`, and
`publish_candidate_plan` commits **one** file at a pinned ref. A create-new project is a
tree. Repairing only the increment would publish a revision whose roadmap still holds the
bytes admission refused, and the other documents would be unrestorable because they never
had a draft. So the create-new repair is a second `CREATE_NEW_PROJECT` stage over the
published revision, with the allowlist narrowed to the pair admission read.

**The narrowing travels on the dispatch, not as a parameter.** My first attempt threaded
a sixth argument through `_run_cli_stage` -> `_build_run_tool_registry` ->
`_build_role_registry` -> `build_planner_registry` -> `_build_tool_builders` ->
`_build_limited_write`. That is five chances to drop it and five signatures to keep in
step for one narrower tuple, and I abandoned it mid-way (reverted with
`git checkout`). `PlannerDispatch` already reaches every layer, so the scope rides there
as `repair_allowlist`, validated in `__post_init__`: every entry inside `authoring_root`,
non-empty, and only on the authoring kind. A dispatch that cannot describe its own scope
is refused before a stage exists, which is the same shape the rest of that class uses.

**What is repairable is a decision, not a default.** `bootstrap-collision` is a fact
about the workspace, not about the bytes -- repairing it would ask the planner to author
into a directory it does not own, which is how a repair becomes an overwrite. `unavailable`
is about the authority, so a second stage fails identically. `bootstrap-refused` is the
repair stage's own failure, and a failed repair is not repaired by another. Only content
refusals (`invalid-metadata`, `invalid-body`, and the disposition rules) are eligible.

**Budget had nowhere to live.** The shared `_WorkflowAdmission.planner_calls` counter
cannot bound this: on the create-new route admission authority is created *by* the
refusal being repaired, so at the first repair there is no counter object at all. One
integer (`authored_repairs`) on the frozen context, bounded by `replans_allowed`, which is
the existing operator-facing knob -- no new budget concept.

Tests: `test_a_create_new_repair_may_write_only_the_documents_admission_read` (the roadmap
and ledger are refused with `path_denied`, the writer is the one the model actually sees),
`test_a_repair_allowlist_outside_the_authoring_root_is_refused_at_construction` (outside
root, empty, and wrong-kind), `test_a_create_new_repair_is_budgeted_and_never_overwrites_on_collision`
(four non-repairable rules, two repairable, and exhaustion). Two mutants killed: disabling
the narrowing (`if False and ...`) and making the budget unconditional.

**Not yet proved end-to-end.** No test drives a live planner through a refusal and a
successful second stage; that needs a provider double honest at the tool level, and I would
rather say so than write a test that asserts the wiring I just built. TEST-2.8's full claim
stays absent for that reason.

355 tests across nine banks, 221 across the controller/CLI/e2e six; ruff clean, mypy 224
clean, doc-links 370 OK.

### E593 — D-V2-9.9: a repair stage writes no scaffold (2026-11-21)

The rule was already written down and I had just broken it. D-V2-9.9 says the scaffold
file set is the *only* harness write and that "a second authoring stage (repair) writes no
scaffold at all". The repair stage I landed in E592 used `CREATE_NEW_PROJECT` -- and
`_seed_scaffold_if_authoring` selects on exactly that kind. So every repair would have run
the scaffold writer.

**It would not have failed loudly; it would have failed fatally.** `_write_project_scaffold`
writes with `expected_sha256=None`, which in this port means *expect absence* -- that is
the mechanism that turns a colliding project into `STALE_REVISION` instead of an overwrite
(D-V2-9.2). On a repair, every scaffold file already exists, so `roadmap.md` -- written
first, deliberately -- would refuse the whole stage. The repair feature could never have
run once, and the symptom would have been a create-new run that refused, repaired,
refused, and reported `bootstrap-refused` with no hint that the harness was the problem.

**Where the fix belongs.** Not in `_run_create_new_repair` (it would have to remember to
suppress a write another layer owns), and not in `_write_project_scaffold` (it would have
to ask whether it is allowed to do its one job). The predicate that *chooses* the stage
already reads the dispatch, and the dispatch already carries `repair_allowlist`, so the
seed function distinguishes the two stages in one condition. That is the seam: a repair is
a create-new stage that is narrower, and "narrower" is already a fact on the object.

**The test had to prove silence.** A double that refuses writes would have passed for the
wrong reason, so the double accepts every write and the test asserts the list is empty. It
also asserts the *first* stage writes exactly the seven scaffold files in order --
otherwise "wrote nothing" could be satisfied by a seed function that no longer works.

Mutant: `if False and planner_dispatch.repair_allowlist is not None` -> killed by
`assert [('worklogs/...scaffold body...'), ...] == []`.

**Sandbox note (new, and it cost real time).** The session's sandbox was re-created with
Python 3.11 while the project requires >=3.13, and `release-assets.githubusercontent.com`
is blocked, so no matching interpreter can be installed. `src/` is 3.11-clean except
`typing.override` (shimmed from `typing_extensions` in the venv, never in the repo); four
test modules use PEP 695 *syntax*, so the suite runs from a rewritten `/tmp` overlay and
the repository's `tests/` is untouched. **A run in this sandbox is not the project gate.**
Two consequences worth recording: `tests/test_s8_workflow_controller.py` fails 11 tests
here both before and after my change (the pty pool needs `tmux`, which is absent), and
`mypy src/` reports 12 `unused-ignore` errors that are identical on an untouched tree
(3.13 needs those ignores; 3.11 does not). Neither is attributable to this work.

### E594 — TEST-2.8 e2e: a refused project is repaired in place (2026-11-21)

E592 ended with an honest gap: the repair mechanism was built but nothing drove a live
planner through a refusal and a successful second stage. This closes it with two real
stages against the real authority -- no doubles at the seam that matters.

**Case.** Stage 1 publishes a project whose geometry is right and whose *pair* disagrees:
the increment says `Roadmap-ID: RM-somewhere-else` while the roadmap beside it says
`RM-repair-project`. `parse_plan` accepts the grammar; `check_project_metadata` is what
refuses, which is exactly the D-V2-9.3 claim -- the cross-check moved into admission, so it
is admission that must catch this, not the renderer that no longer exists. Stage 2 reopens
a WRITE view at that published revision, rewrites the increment, and admission binds the
result.

**What the measured behaviour added.** I first probed whether a second WRITE view could
open at all in the same managed environment, because an earlier note in this session said
it could not. It can -- but *only* after the D-V2-9.9 fix: the probe failed at
`WorkspacePortError: stale` before it, and returned `update-ok` / `update-ok` after. So the
scaffold bug was not a latent hygiene issue; it was the thing that made two-stage repair
impossible, and the note that said "do not retry a second stage" was measuring that bug
rather than a platform limit.

**Mutation.** M1 replaces `check_project_metadata(...)` with `pass` -- KILLED: the first
stage would admit and the test's `bootstrap-invalid-metadata` assertion catches it. A
second mutant that weakened the repair allowlist did not apply (pattern matched 0 times);
rather than fake a kill I left it out. The e2e's discriminating power against the repair
path itself is therefore proven by M1 plus the earlier unit-level allowlist mutants.

**Guarded against false success.** Before the refusal check the test asserts the revision
actually moved, so a stage that failed to publish cannot satisfy `refusal is not None` for
the wrong reason.

**Sandbox lesson, recorded because it cost most of a session.** The sandbox was rebuilt on
Python 3.11 while the project targets 3.13, and I spent the session building a shim and a
rewritten test overlay -- none of which was needed: `scripts/arena-env-build.sh` builds the
pinned CPython 3.13.16 and the frozen dev environment, and after running it the suite,
`ruff` and `mypy` all pass natively. The 11 `test_s8_workflow_controller` failures and the
12 `mypy unused-ignore` errors I classified as environmental were purely 3.11 artifacts and
are gone on 3.13.16 (26 passed; mypy 224 clean). Use the project's own build script before
diagnosing the environment.

### E595 — the e2e proved repair was possible, not that the path did it (2026-11-21)

E594's e2e assembled the second stage by hand: it ran stage 1, called
`_admit_published_project`, then built its own `PlannerDispatch` for the repair. Every
assertion passed. Mutation M3 -- "the repair runs with no narrowed scope" -- replaced
`repair_allowlist=_repair_allowlist(root)` with `None` inside `_run_create_new_repair` and
**survived**. The mutant is a real weakening: an unbounded repair could rewrite the roadmap
and publish a project admission never read.

The reason is the one worth remembering: the test never executed the code it was supposed
to protect. It proved repair is *possible*, which is a property of the pieces, not of the
bound path. A test that builds the machinery it is checking cannot fail when that machinery
is deleted.

**The fix is a second test, not a stronger first one.** `test_the_bound_repair_path_runs_
both_stages_and_binds_the_result` drives `_bind_authored_project` with the production
recursion seam (`run_stage_fn`, the same hook `_cmd_run` supplies through
`invoke_workflow`). Stage 1 is real; stage 2 is dispatched *by the bound path*; the test
records the scope of every dispatch it receives and asserts `scopes == ["narrowed"]`.
M3 dies there. M4 ("the bound path never dispatches a repair", `if False:`) dies there too
-- without it, a green suite would have said nothing about the wiring at all.

**M5 survived and that is correct.** "A repair is not budgeted" is killed by
`test_a_create_new_repair_is_budgeted_and_never_overwrites_on_collision`, a different test
with a different subject. Recorded in the harness comment so nobody later "fixes" a bank
that is already covered, and so the kill attribution stays honest: 5/5 mutants, but not all
from one test.

### E596 — CT-2.7 was the one control with a data-loss failure mode, and nothing proved it (2026-11-21)

Re-checking the plan's citations after E594/E595 left eighteen absent. Seventeen are
SLICE2–SLICE5 work the plan already schedules. CT-2.7 was different: the collision guard is
*already implemented* (`_authoring_collision` plus create-only scaffold writes), so its
absence was not a schedule -- it was an untested property with the worst failure mode in the
set. "Create over an existing project" that is only *mostly* refused overwrites someone
else's work.

**What the test pins, and why each half is separate.** The guard has two independent
mechanisms and either alone can rot:

* the *decision* reads the pinned inventory and refuses before dispatch. Checked against a
  live-shaped inventory, including the case the plan calls out explicitly -- an **incomplete**
  `worklogs/<slug>/` collides too, because a create may not finish a tree it did not start;
* the *write* is create-only (`expected_sha256=None`). Checked against the real authority by
  running a second create of the same slug and comparing the published tree byte for byte.

The ordering assertion is the one I did not plan and the measurement added: `reached == []`.
The second create is refused *before the planner runs*, so a doomed run never spends a
provider call. Had the guard been at the write site only, this would have caught it.

**Mutants** (all killed, in `tests/mutation/mut_test_28.py`, now 8/8): the collision check
disabled; the incomplete-directory case treated as free; the scaffold switched to "expect a
known sha", which is what an overwrite would look like.

**Honest scope.** This is CT-2.7 only. TEST-2.2 (invalid input refuses before provider),
TEST-2.3 (scaffold then write inside the slug) and TEST-2.5 (child failure mapping) remain
absent, and CT-2.4 remains blocked on SLICE2's seal. They are the next items of this class,
in that order -- 2.2 before 2.3 because 2.2 is the one that can overwrite.

### E597 — CT-2.2: the control is the ordering, so the test measures ordering (2026-11-21)

The plan's row says "invalid slug, traversal and malformed route refuse before provider".
Every word of that is about *when*, not *what*, so a test asserting the error code would
have proved the smaller half. These assert `workflow.calls == []`: the child run is never
invoked. That is observable, it cannot be satisfied by a message, and it distinguishes
"validated" from "validated too late" -- which for traversal is the whole question.

**Ten slug shapes**, chosen so each one fails for a different reason rather than piling up
near-duplicates: uppercase, underscore, space, empty, over the 48-character limit, two
traversal spellings (`../escape`, `worklogs/../etc`), a nested traversal, and both dash
edges. `worklogs/../etc` is the one worth naming: it is long enough to look like a path and
contains no `..` as a whole component, so it exercises the regex rather than an obvious
`startswith` check.

**Two route refusals beside it**, because "malformed route" is the other half of the row:
a slug with no create route (ambiguous -- dropping it would select a project the caller did
not name, honouring it would create one they did not ask for) and an unknown
`project_action` (which must not fall through to the `AUTO_SELECT_EXISTING` default, where
"create" misspelled becomes "select").

**Mutants**, all killed: the slug regex not enforced; a route-less slug silently dropped;
an unknown action falling through to the default. Harness now 11/11.

**Where the test lives, and why.** Not in `test_ai_native_bootstrap.py` as the plan's row
first spelled it, but beside the other `invoke_workflow` validation tests -- this is the
tool's public field validation, and putting it in the bootstrap bank would have separated
it from the fixture (`_RecordingWorkflow`) that makes the ordering observable. The plan row
now cites both halves separately.

**Remaining of this class:** TEST-2.3 (scaffold then write inside the slug) and TEST-2.5
(child failure mapping). CT-2.4 stays blocked on SLICE2's seal.
