### E682 — source audit: project freshness, origin and STEP9A remainder (2026-11-23)

Source review, not an implementation or new runtime/mutation result. `register_new` creates
an absent workspace root but can copy an approved seed; `register_existing` snapshots an
existing root, and `_register` writes the initial revision/current/workspace metadata
without any project history. Neither a new workspace binding nor the present absence of a
`worklogs/<slug>` directory establishes that the slug has never had a seal. In particular,
a state-lost, re-registered existing workspace must not acquire a fresh-history proof just
because its current snapshot is empty. Coherent rollback of all coordinated state remains
outside the already-ratified MVP scope; state loss or unprovable provenance is not evidence
of freshness.

The authoring path seeds through the stage's WRITE port (`cli.py::_seed_scaffold_if_authoring`)
and finishes via ordinary REVISION publication; the immutable REVISION intent explicitly has
`target_relative=None`, and recovery distinguishes pre/post pointer using `current.json`.
`_record_acceptance_origin` is called only by completed BOOTSTRAP install/recovery, not that
REVISION path. E679 is a real-service witness for the resulting refusal. The controller's
`_seal_published_project` and `_stage_acceptance_bundle` still use `SealStore(ctx.workspace)`;
private store/read transport does not yet replace them and E657 remains false.

BOOTSTRAP's `RENAME_NOREPLACE` establishes absence at the instant of install, not absence
throughout a workspace's history. `install_project` checks the live destination and
`_record_acceptance_origin` creates the per-project origin if absent; the current source
has no independent workspace-wide tombstone/history check on this branch. **Potential
loss/recreate gap, source inference only:** if an old project is validly removed by a
permitted unbound publication and its origin/private evidence is lost, a later install of
the same slug appears able to create a fresh origin. Existing real-bootstrap loss test
covers loss followed by re-registration while the project still exists, not this sequence.
Before claiming or fixing the gap, reproduce the full public authority lifecycle and any
applicable publication restrictions; do not call it experimentally confirmed yet.
Likewise the acceptance-boundary validator is conditional on a plan-bound ordinary seal,
not a global proof of all project creation/deletion routes.

Recommended candidate (subject to implementation proof): a durable authority-private,
workspace-bound monotonic project-history/coverage anchor, initialized only at a trusted
registration/provisioning boundary and never auto-created for an already-existing binding
with unknown history. Registration snapshots every relevant pre-existing project as
historical/unknown, including seed contents; treat untrusted re-registration/legacy
bindings as unknown, not fresh, unless restored/recovered with adequate independent proof.
A history entry/tombstone is never deleted when a project disappears. Authority-controlled
creation is allowed only against complete valid history and reserves a never-seen slug;
its durable operation identity, base/next revision and history transition must be tied to
REVISION and BOOTSTRAP forward/recovery semantics. All creation/deletion paths, malformed
entries, bounds, replay, concurrent and crash paths need coverage; choose exact storage
representation after checking existing constraints, not a second independent trust service.
If history/coverage is lost, refuse automatic mint/provisioning; preserve the ratified
coordinated backup/restore and W4 witness. No guarantee against a coherent rollback of the
entire coordinated state is implied. An explicit authority-scoped bootstrap operation for
staged authoring is an alternative, but cannot avoid historical-slug proof or recovery by
itself, and must preserve the staged authoring/repair workflow.

STEP9A remainder: (1) project history/origin and recovery plus real fresh-stage private
store/read integration and uncertainty fences; (2) independently trustworthy collection,
complete closure/runner binding and authority semantic provenance; (3) actual coder-visible
mode-A shell/file read-only projection, ancestor/alias/ABA defenses and same-closure
verification, with isolated immutable-payload fallback when revision strategy cannot be
proved; (4) pre-code exact-assertion sensitivity and baseline/error classification;
(5) production exact mutation attribution, evidence, observe/enforce integrity routing;
(6) TEST-DEFECT authorization, planner disposition, new seal/revision and retained evidence;
(7) real-route positive/adversarial and durable-effect/no-effect tests including mode-B
refusal; (8) E674 full `just check` and complete per-module mutation sweep/review. Some
component tests and transport already exist but none alone establishes end-to-end custody.
STEP9B, new slices and W4 are subsequent distinct gates, not extra STEP9A closure claims.

### E683 — operator amendment: explicit lifecycle recovery (2026-11-23)

The operator selected the prior discussion's practical deletion/reset policy. Trusted
project deletion closes an incarnation and releases its slug; re-creation uses a distinct
incarnation/evidence lineage. For a live project with lost seal state, trusted explicit
recovery may revalidate current plan, complete closure, collection and pre-code gates,
then establish a new seal/evidence lineage. Old verification/mutation results are not
credited; current bytes are not claimed to restore lost bytes. Manual out-of-band deletion
must be reconciled through authority. Coder removal of files cannot silently self-authorize
reset. Exact old history can instead be recovered via coordinated backup/restore; W4
witness remains required, coherent complete rollback outside MVP. This supersedes E669's
blanket fail-closed/no-remint and E682's proposed permanent slug-history requirement,
while preserving no silent remint, TEST-DEFECT lineage, custody and E657. Plan, parent
increment and custody design are amended; policy is decided, implementation is open.

Source implications: `_owner_only` checks run capability/active namespace/UID:GID, not
planner versus coder or explicit human authorization. A trusted management edge must be
defined and tested before offering reset; don't add an OWNER-only reset and assume it is a
separate capability. The current bundle's deterministic canonical hash and
`VerificationIdentity` lack an incarnation ID (`test_the_same_inputs_always_mint_the_same_bytes`);
unchanged bytes and unchanged revision can recreate the old digest. New lineage must be
authority-issued and actually checked by evidence consumers, not just logged. This does not
require an external history service; choose the representation after threat/recovery review.
The V2 plan records the creation/deletion/manual-drift/loss/replay/restore matrix. No
recovery, fresh origin, independent collection, mode A or host PASS is claimed.

### E684 — distinguish blocked PIN from uncertain PIN; publication fence (2026-11-23)

E681 conservatively retained a child slot when the parent seal fence rejected the PIN before
transport, confusing a pending *other* operation with an uncertain PIN. `pin_reader` now
raises an `ExecutionUncertainError` subtype specifically for its local pre-send guard,
preserving operation ID and any pending candidate handle; the child tool reports unavailable
and releases its active slot only for that type. An actual lost PIN response still retains the
slot. Managed reader, project/candidate view, candidate read, revision diff and stage publish
also now refuse locally while candidate publication is unresolved; a lost reply may already

use a fake client; this is not concurrency or durable controller-process recovery proof.

### E685 — prevent identity-changing seal load and stale in-memory store (2026-11-23)

While preparing E683 incarnation/lineage, a source review found that the record loader
accepted a rehashed unknown top-level field, duplicate JSON keys, duplicate identity names,
and noncanonical bytes. A C3 test reproduced the concrete first case with private state,
real authority, service and client over AF_UNIX: the pointer named the forged digest,
but the service serialized the parsed object after dropping the unknown field and the
client accepted a *different* digest. This required alteration of authority-private state;
we do not claim an unprivileged coder could perform it. The tests failed before the fix.

`acceptance_bundle.load_seal` now requires the exact canonical bytes of the validated
returned bundle, refuses duplicate identity labels and noncanonical identity ordering,
and classifies parser recursion as malformed. Thus no ignored field, duplicate key,
alternate encoding or sorted-field normalization can silently change the seal on read.
`SealStore.store` also checks the serialized bundle round-trip equals the incoming object
before any directory, record or pointer write: a stale `seal_sha256` previously permitted a
record under the wrong name/pointer. Tests cover fresh and existing pointers with no extra
or modified artifacts. This tightens the stated canonical-record contract; manually
pretty-printed or otherwise noncanonical old records now fail closed rather than being
silently normalized. The canonical writer already emits accepted bytes; no migration for
noncanonical external records is claimed.

C3 real-service/UDS tests prove unknown field, duplicate key, duplicate identity and
noncanonical records return CORRUPT_STATE without changing pointer/record; the origin is a
synthetic fixture and not fresh-project evidence. C0 adds unordered identity; both fresh
and existing store cases assert no mutation. TEST-EDITS: extended existing bundle, seal
store, and service tests; existing assertions retained. Four manual mutants killed:
canonical validation at UDS caller edge, duplicate identity at UDS, ordering guard, and
store pre-effect roundtrip. Restored all. Final 16-module bank **1067 passed**;
Ruff/format, scoped mypy for the two production modules, environment check and diff pass.
This hardens identity integrity needed for E683 but does **not** issue an incarnation,
authorize recovery, wire controller private custody or prove mode A. STEP9A, E657, full
`just check`, all-module mutation sweep and W4 remain open.

### E686 — operator selects writable working artifacts; nested scope question (2026-11-23)

Operator accepted the adversarial review: agents should edit/append project ledger, notes
and e2e without reseal or undeserved file-tool denials; shell and file tools must agree,
and design must minimize late seal/publication refusal and lost unrelated work. Project
ledger and editable E2E documents are not authoritative PASS: a live verdict requires a
recorded execution and an assigned reviewer. Planner authors acceptance before sealing;
coder reads but cannot edit it, and TEST-DEFECT creates a new revision. Seal demonstrates
identity, not test quality. The operator accepts the risk of plans referencing mutable
notes; this does not prove closure integrity or let mutable reports forge PASS.

Source audit: `sealed_project_paths` protects all of `worklogs/<slug>` for file IO;
WRITE profile mounts the workspace RW for shell, while ordinary publication protects
plan path and acceptance, so the interfaces are not equivalent. E672 demonstrates that
an acceptance-only nested RO bind loses against writable ancestor rename; broad worklogs
RO prevents requested working writes. `publication._validate_mutation_roots` separately
limits nested `MUTATION` coder to src/scripts, per ratified Q141=C (E527). Thus universal
working writes conflict with existing nested boundary; **Q-V2-WRITE-SCOPE-1 is OPEN**
with options and recommendation in V2 plan. No silent weakening or exception has landed.

V2 plan, parent STEP9A and custody design record policy, selective-projection experiment,

and W4 ledger-append plus no-forged-PASS host cases. Q-V2-LEDGER-1 policy is resolved;

is claimed. E657 remains active; E683/E674, STEP9A/9B and W4 remain open.

### E688 — selective mount candidate fails ledger write continuity (2026-11-23)

E687 prototype reused the E672 user/mount namespace harness. RO worklogs with RW notes,
e2e and *file* bind ledger initially allows append, notes atomic rename and e2e writes while
acceptance write/project rename fail. The parent outside the namespace performs a real
`RootedViewIO` read and atomic expected-digest replacement on `view/source`-shaped storage.
The child sees replacement bytes, but its next append fails EROFS. A shell temp file beside
ledger fails EROFS and replace from a notes mount fails EXDEV. Parent source reads establish
the resulting ledger/notes/e2e bytes. Thus this particular candidate fails agreed working
write continuity and is not a production solution. The first experiment attempted replacement
inside the same namespace and got EBUSY; corrected to use a parent outside the namespace.
The result is limited to this filesystem/kernel/test topology; no Docker, actual authority
snapshot/publish, alias/ABA, production C1 or host proof is claimed.
